[PhilidorNote "Philidor sets this game out beginning with the Black; the sides are exchanged here so that the first player moves as White."]

1. e4 {The king's pawn, two steps.} e5 {The same.} 2. Nf3 {The king's knight, at his bishop's
third square.} d6 {The queen's pawn, one move.} 3. Bc4 {The king's bishop, at his queen's
bishop's fourth square.} f5 {The king's bishop's pawn, two moves. (a) NOTE: It is always
advantageous to change your king's bishop's pawn for his royal pawn; because, by that means,
your king's and queen's pawns can place themselves in the centre of the chess-board: besides, in
castling on your right wing, your rook finds itself free and fit for action in the very
beginning of the game, as will be demonstrated by a back-game on the same play.} 4. d3 {The
queen's pawn, one move.} c6 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} 5. exf5 {The king's pawn
takes the pawn. (b) NOTE: If your adversary refuses taking your bishop's pawn, you are to leave
it in the same place and situation, exposed to be taken, and not to push it on, till he has
castled; and you must afterwards, with the pawns of your right wing, form your attack upon the
pawns which cover his king, as is explained in a back-game on that move. You are to observe
again, as a general rule, not to determine easily to push on the pawns, either of your right or
left wing, before your adversary's king has castled; because he will otherwise retire on the
side where your pawns are less advanced, and consequently less dangerous to him.} Bxf5 {The
queen's bishop retakes the pawn.} 6. Bg5 {The queen's bishop, at the adverse king's knight's
fourth square.} Nf6 {The king's knight, at his bishop's third square.} 7. Nbd2 {The queen's
knight, at his queen's second square. (c) NOTE: If he takes your knight with his bishop, you
must absolutely take his with your pawn, to bring the strength of your pawns towards the
centre.} d5 {The queen's pawn, one move.} 8. Bb3 {The bishop retires. Qk.3.19} Bd6 {The king's
bishop, at his queen's third square. (d) NOTE: This is the best square your king's bishop can
chuse, except the fourth of your queen's bishop: in that place he may be of. great service to
you, to form your attack upon his king's rook's pawn, in case he castles on his left side.} 9.
Qe2 {The queen, at her king's second square.} Qe7 {The same.} 10. O-O {The king castles on his
rook's side. (e) NOTE: If he had castled on his queen's side, it would have been then your game
to castle on your king's side, in order to attack him afterwards more easily with your pawns on
the left. It is here again necessary to observe for a general rule, that, as it is very often
dangerous to attack the adversary too soon, it must serve likewise for instruction here, not to
be too hasty in your attack, till your pawns are previously sustained by one another, and also
by your pieces; otherwise those hasty attacks will prove abortive, as will be seen by a back-
game on this play.} Nbd7 {The queen's knight, at his queen's second square.} 11. Nh4 {The king's
knight, at his rook's fourth square. (f) NOTE: He plays the knight to make room for his king's
bishop's pawn, with a design to advance it two steps, in order to strive to break the line of
your pawns.} Qe6 {The queen, at her king's third square.} 12. Nxf5 {The king's knight takes the
bishop. (g) NOTE: If he had pushed his king's bishop's. pawn two steps, instead of taking your
bishop, you should then have attacked his queen with your queen's bishop, and pushed your king's
rook's pawn the next move upon his bishor, to force him to take your knight: in this case your
best way was to retake his bißop with your pawn, in order the better to support your royal pawn,
and replace i in case it be taken.} Qxf5 {The queen retakes the knight. E $.} 13. Bxf6 {The
queen's bishop takes the knight. (h) NOTE: If he did not take this knight, his bishop would
remain imprisoned by your pawns; or he would lose three moves, which loss would entirely ruin
his games.} gxf6 {The pawn retakes the bishop.} 14. f4 {The king's bishop's pawn, two moves.}
Qg6 {The queen, at her king's knight's third square.} 15. fxe5 {The king's bishop's pawn takes
the pawn.} fxe5 {The bishop's pawn retakes it.} 16. Rf3 {The king's rook, at its king's bishop's
third square. (i) NOTE: He plays this rook with two designs; either to attack and remove your
queen, or to double it, as the case may require, with his other rook.} h5 {The king's rook's
pawn, two steps. (k) NOTE: You push this pawn two steps, to give room to your queen, in case
your adversary attacks her with his king's rook.} 17. Raf1 {The queen's rook, at its king's
bishop's square.} O-O-O {The king castles on his queen's side.} 18. c4 {The queen's bishop's
pawn, two steps.} e4 {The king's pawn, one step. (l) NOTE: Here is a move, as difficult to
comprehend, as it is to be well explained. In the first place, you are to observe, that, when
you find yourself with a chain of pawns following one another, the pawn which is at the head of
them must strive to preserve its post. Your king's pawn not being upon the same-coloured
squares, or in oblique line with the others, your adversary has pushed his queen's bishop's
pawn, for two reasons; the first, to engage you to push that of your queen forwards, which would
then be stopped by that of his queen's, and by that means to bring about that your king's pawn,
being left behind, should become useless to you; the second is, to hinder at the same time your
king's bishop from battering upon his king's rook's pawn; therefore you ought to push your
king's pawn forwards upon his rook, and even sacrifice it, because your adversary, by taking it,
opens a free passage to Diij the pawns of your queen, which you are to advance immediately, and
sustain, in case of need, with your others, in order to endeavour to make a queen with it, or
draw some other considerable advantage by it, to win the game. It is true, that his queen's
pawn, being now on the same line with its king, appears to have the same advantage, of having no
opposition from your pawns, to make a queen: however, the difference is great, because his pawn
being entirely separated, and incapable of being united and sustained by any of the others, will
always be in danger of being seized on in its road by any of your pieces at war with it. This
move, as I observed before, is very difficult; and one must be already a good player to judge
well of it.} 19. dxe4 {The queen's pawn takes the pawn.} d4 {The queen's pawn, one move.} 20.
Bc2 {The bishop, at his queen's bishop's second square.} Ne5 {The knight, at his king's fourth
square. (m) NOTE: It was necessary to play this knight, in order to stop his king's pawn; the
rather, because this very pawn, in its present situation, stops the passage of his own bishop,
and even of his knight.} 21. Rf6 {The king's rook, at the adverse king's bishop's third square.}
Qg7 {The queen, at her king's knight's second square.} 22. Qf2 {The queen, at her king's
bishop's second square. (n) knight NOTE: He plays his queen, in order afterwards to give check;
but, instead of playing her, if he had pushed his king's rook's pawn, to hinder the attack of
your knight, you must have pushed one step your queen's pawn, which would have ensured you the
game.} Ng4 {The knight, at the adverse king's knight's fourth square.} 23. Qf5+ {The queen gives
check.} Kb8 {The king, at his queen's knight's square.} 24. Rxd6 {The rook takes the bishop. (o)
NOTE: He takes this bishop to save his king's rook's pawn; the rather, because that bishop
proves more incommodious to him than all your other pieces, and by this play he keeps in check
your queen's rook with his queen.} Rxd6 {The rook retakes the rook.} 25. Qf4 {The queen, at her
king's bishop's fourth square.} Qe5 {The queen, at her king's fourth square. (p) NOTE: Having
the advantage of a rook against a bishop, at the end of a party, it is your advantage to change
the queen, because his queen is troublesome to you in her present situation; and to avoid the
checkmate, he finds himself under the necessity of taking her.} 26. Qxe5 {The queen takes the
queen.} Nxe5 {The knight retakes the queen.} 27. Rf5 {The rook, at the adverse king's bishop's
fourth square.} Ng4 {The knight, at the adverse king's knight's fourth square.} 28. c5 {The
queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} Rg6 {The queen's rook, at her king's knight's third square.}
29. Nc4 {The knight, at his queen's bishop's fourth square.} Ne3 {The knight, at the adverse
king's third square.} 30. Nxe3 {The knight takes the knight.} dxe3 {The pawn retakes the
knight.} 31. Rf3 {The rook, at its king's bishop's third square.} Rd8 {The king's rook, at its
queen's square. (q) NOTE: You must make yourself master of the openings, to make the rooks fit
for action, especially at the end of a game.} 32. Rxe3 {The rook takes the pawn.} Rd2 {The
king's rook, at the adverse queen's second square, and wins the game. [ 41 1} *
